attachments.origin_landmark: greater wing (superior head); lateral pterygoid plate (inferior head)

actions: protrudes mandible, depresses chin (opens jaw), guides TMJ disc during movement

functional_compartments.name: Superior head
functional_compartments.function_note: Inserts mainly onto the TMJ disc/capsule; classically described as predominantly active during jaw CLOSING/clenching (stabilizing the disc against the condyle) -- the standard teaching model of an opposite-phase functional split from the inferior head, though more recent EMG-with-imaging studies have found the reciprocal activity pattern less clear-cut than this classical model suggests (see source note).
functional_compartments.source: Murray GM, Phanachet I, Uchida S, Whittle T (2004) Aust Dent J 49(1):2-8 -- review of the lateral pterygoid's two-head anatomy and the classical reciprocal-activity model (superior head active during jaw closing/clenching, inferior head during opening/protrusion); note that later EMG-with-imaging-verified studies (Murray et al. (2001) J Neurophysiol 86:1595-1602) found less clear-cut reciprocal activity than the classical model suggests, so this functional split is presented here as the standard teaching model rather than a settled finding (corrects an earlier draft's attribution of this specific functional claim to van Eijden et al. 1997, an architecture-only study that does not address activity timing -- caught by adversarial fact-check, see docs/VERIFICATION.md)

functional_compartments.name: Inferior head
functional_compartments.function_note: Larger head, inserting mainly onto the condylar neck; classically described as the primary mover for jaw OPENING and protrusion, active in the opposite phase from the superior head per the standard teaching model (see source note on newer EMG findings).
functional_compartments.source: Murray GM, Phanachet I, Uchida S, Whittle T (2004) Aust Dent J 49(1):2-8 -- review of the lateral pterygoid's two-head anatomy and the classical reciprocal-activity model (superior head active during jaw closing/clenching, inferior head during opening/protrusion); note that later EMG-with-imaging-verified studies (Murray et al. ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Extraoral, over the infratemporal region below the zygomatic arch, oriented toward the maxillary tuberosity -- the maxillary tuberosity is reported as the most reliable landmark for guiding needle insertion angle and orientation toward the lateral pterygoid plate/muscle. In cadaveric measurements taken from surface landmarks, the muscle mass sits a mean of 13.5 mm inferior to the tragus (vertical distance) and 34.1 mm from it (transverse distance).
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Mean depth from the zygomatic arch to the muscle was 23.3 mm in cadaveric dissections. The inferior head (the more common EMG/BoNT target) is significantly longer and thicker than the superior head, and lies more laterally and inferiorly relative to the angulus oris, tragus and lateral canthus landmarks.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: A two-headed muscle in 93.3% of specimens; the mean pterygomaxillary angle (between the lateral pterygoid plate and the maxillary tuberosity) is 124.7 +/- 16.6 degrees, most often in the moderately obtuse (type II) range (63.3% of specimens) -- used to orient the needle trajectory.
structures_at_risk: maxillary artery -- courses superficial to the lateral pterygoid in 53.3% of specimens (vs. deep or transitional courses in the remainder), so its position relative to the muscle is variable and not reliably predictable from surface landmarks alone
auriculotemporal and other mandibular-division trigeminal nerve branches, coursing through the infratemporal fossa adjacent to the muscle
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: These figures come from two cadaveric topographic-anatomy studies aimed specifically at improving landmark-guided extraoral access for TMD interventions (including BoNT and dry needling), not from an EMG innervation-zone or motor-endplate mapping study -- no percent-along-a-reference-line motor endplate zone was found for this muscle. Clinically, EMG guidance is also widely used for lateral (and medial) pterygoid BoNT injection because of the muscle's deep, variable location, and ultrasound/CT-segmentation-guided approaches have been used for lateral pterygoid BoNT in anterior disc displacement, but none of those clinical-outcome studies reported a landmark-referenced injection coordinate in the level of anatomic detail captured here.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Karip B, Ok F, Korkmaz Fulya T, Keles P. 'Topographic Anatomy of the Lateral Pterygoid Muscle: Implications for Landmark-Guided Extraoral Interventions.' J Craniofac Surg 37(6):1745-1750 (2026), doi:10.1097/SCS.0000000000012402 (https://doi.org/10.1097/SCS.0000000000012402) -- 30 hemifacial cadaver specimens; Ok F, Karip B, Temizsoy Korkmaz F, Keles P. 'Anatomical relationship between the lateral pterygoid muscle and maxillary artery: Morphological classification and clinical implications.' Cranio 44(5):928-934 (2026), doi:10.1080/08869634.2026.2622431 (https://doi.org/10.1080/08869634.2026.2622431) -- 30 hemifaces. Both retrieved via PubMed.
